title: Phase3 audit gate defaults to signature verification disabled, allowing unsigned checkpoint acceptance
description: Phase3AuditGatePolicy defaults `require_valid_signature` to `false` and `max_allowed_drift_score` to `0.0`. While the drift score default is safe (strict), the signature default means that any deployment using the default Phase3RuntimeConfig will accept audit certificates with no cryptographic signature verification. The ValidatePhase3RuntimeConfig() function enforces that `allowed_signature_algorithms` is non-empty *only when* `require_valid_signature` is true — so the dangerous default path is never caught by validation. An attacker with filesystem write access to the checkpoint store can forge arbitrary audit certificates (with `verdict=kPass, drift_score=0.0`) and they will be accepted by the checkpoint decision gate since no signature check runs.
impact: An attacker who can write to the checkpoint/audit storage can inject fabricated audit certificates that will be trusted by the decision engine. This lets them substitute arbitrary projected memory into DPM decisions, bypassing the entire Phase 3 replay audit trust chain. The attack is silent because unsigned certificates appear identical to legitimate ones in the gate's evaluation logic.
attack_path: 1. Attacker gains write access to the checkpoint/audit store directory (e.g. via shared filesystem, container escape, or supply chain). 2. Attacker crafts a forged AuditCertificate with verdict=kPass, drift_score=0.0, and matching checkpoint_manifest_hash. 3. Attacker writes the encoded certificate to the audit ledger. 4. StatelessDecisionEngine or LoadAuditedProjectionCheckpointForDecision loads the checkpoint — the decision gate sees a passing audit certificate and does not require signatures. 5. The forged checkpoint's projected memory is used for the next DPM decision.
evidence: runtime/dpm/phase3_runtime_config.cc:36-41 — signature algorithms only validated when require_valid_signature is true
remediation: Change the default of `require_valid_signature` to `true` in Phase3AuditGatePolicy and AuditedProjectionCheckpointRequest. Add a validation rule in ValidatePhase3RuntimeConfig that requires at least one allowed_signature_algorithms entry unconditionally (or fail if require_valid_signature is false). Document in comments that disabling signature verification is only acceptable for test environments.
poc_video_notes: Create a Phase3RuntimeConfig with all defaults, show that ApplyPhase3RuntimeConfig succeeds, then demonstrate that a forged unsigned AuditCertificate passes the CheckpointDecisionGate evaluation.

title: Projection error message leaks raw untrusted input prefix into correction payloads, enabling log injection
description: In CanonicalizeProjectionJson() at line 105, when JSON parsing fails, the error message includes a 512-byte prefix of the raw model output: `std::string(raw_projection).substr(0, 512)`. This raw_projection string originates from the LLM inference runner, which processes user-supplied event payloads. The error message propagates into the projection replay auditor (projection_replay_auditor.cc line 272-273), where it is hashed as `replay_error` and can flow into CorrectionPayload.correction_text and CorrectionPayload.replacement_projection. These correction payloads are subsequently injected into future projection prompts via FormatProjectionCorrectionDirectives(). An attacker who crafts event payloads that cause the LLM to emit malformed JSON with embedded prompt-injection directives can have those directives persist as correction text.
impact: Attacker-controlled content from malformed projection outputs can be laundered through the correction pipeline and injected into future projection prompts. This creates a persistent prompt injection vector: correction_text containing attacker directives will be included verbatim in all subsequent DPM projections for the affected session, potentially biasing or overriding the projected memory used for decisions.
attack_path: 1. Attacker injects a user event with payload designed to make the LLM emit invalid JSON containing embedded prompt instructions (e.g. `{IGNORE_PREVIOUS: ... new system instruction ...`). 2. CanonicalizeProjectionJson fails to parse and includes the first 512 bytes in the error. 3. Replay auditor hashes the error string, detects drift, and emits a CorrectionPayload whose correction_text/replacement_projection contains the attacker's raw text. 4. On next projection with corrections, FormatProjectionCorrectionDirectives renders the correction_text into the prompt preamble. 5. The LLM follows the injected instructions in correction_text.
evidence: runtime/dpm/dpm_projector.cc:104-106 — raw_projection prefix included in error message
runtime/dpm/projection_replay_auditor.cc:317-323 — replay_error is written as replacement_projection and correction_text
runtime/dpm/dpm_projector.cc:126-136 — correction repair prompt includes correction_directives verbatim
remediation: Sanitize or redact the raw_projection prefix before including it in any error message. Use a constant error string that describes the failure type without echoing untrusted content. Alternatively, apply content-sanitization to all correction_text before it is rendered into prompts (e.g. strip prompt-structural markers, limit character set). Never propagate raw LLM output into correction payloads without sanitization.
poc_video_notes: Submit an event designed to make the LLM return non-JSON output containing `[CORRECTION DIRECTIVE] ...` text. Show the error is captured and persisted as correction_text, then show a subsequent projection prompt that includes the injected text.

title: Uncontrolled memory allocation from attacker-controlled parent_count field in DAG node deserialization
description: In LocalMerkleDagStore::Get() at line 172-180, the parent_count field is read as an arbitrary uint32_t from the on-disk dagnode file. The code then iterates parent_count times, each time push_back()-ing a 32-byte Hash256 into a vector. There is no upper-bound check on parent_count during deserialization (the 0xFFFF check only exists in Put()). A corrupted or maliciously crafted dagnode file with parent_count set to a large value (up to 2^32 - 1) would cause the code to attempt allocation of up to 128 GiB of memory (4 billion * 32 bytes). Even though the view.size() check at line 174 will eventually catch a truncated file, the std::vector reallocation pattern means the runtime will attempt exponential reallocations as it push_back's, causing OOM before the size check fires.
impact: An attacker who can write a crafted .dagnode file to the provenance store can cause the DPM runtime to allocate unbounded memory during deserialization, leading to denial of service via OOM. In constrained environments (e.g. on-device inference, containers with memory limits), this crashes the DPM process. The provenance query (GetCheckpointProvenance) transitively calls Get() for each node in the traversal, amplifying the attack.
attack_path: 1. Attacker gains write access to the DAG store directory (same prerequisite as checkpoint forgery — shared filesystem). 2. Attacker writes a crafted .dagnode file with valid magic header, valid self-hash, but parent_count = 0xFFFFFFFF and minimal trailing data. 3. Any provenance query or audit operation that calls LocalMerkleDagStore::Get() for this node triggers unbounded vector growth. 4. The process is killed by OOM or the memory allocator throws std::bad_alloc (uncaught, terminates).
evidence: runtime/platform/provenance/local_merkle_dag_store.cc:172-180 — parent_count loop with no upper bound during Get()
runtime/platform/provenance/local_merkle_dag_store.cc:105-107 — Put() bounds parent_hashes.size() to 0xFFFF, but Get() does not
runtime/platform/provenance/provenance_query.cc:51-52 — GetCheckpointProvenance calls store.Get() in a loop
remediation: Add an upper-bound validation on parent_count in the Get() deserialization path, matching the 0xFFFF limit enforced in Put(). Before the loop, check `if (parent_count > 0xFFFF) return DataLossError(...)`. Also reserve the vector to prevent incremental reallocation: `node.parent_hashes.reserve(parent_count)` after the bounds check.
poc_video_notes: Craft a binary .dagnode file with parent_count = 0xFFFFFFFF, write it to the DAG store directory, then call GetCheckpointProvenance targeting that node. Monitor memory usage to show unbounded allocation.

title: DurablyWriteFile TOCTOU race allows checkpoint content substitution
description: DurablyWriteFile implements an atomic write pattern (write-to-temp, fsync, rename). However, the callers in LocalFilesystemCheckpointStore and LocalMerkleDagStore implement idempotent-put by first calling ReadEntireFileIfExists() to check for existing content, then calling DurablyWriteFile() if the file does not exist. This creates a TOCTOU (time-of-check-time-of-use) race: between the exists-check and the rename in DurablyWriteFile, a concurrent writer (or attacker) can create the target file. Since rename() replaces existing files atomically, DurablyWriteFile will silently overwrite whatever was placed there. For content-addressed stores this means a last-writer-wins scenario where the 'wrong' content could be stored at a given hash address.
impact: In a concurrent environment (multiple DPM processes sharing a checkpoint directory, or an attacker racing against the runtime), the non-atomic check-then-write pattern allows: (1) Two legitimate writers racing can produce a state where the idempotent-put guarantee is violated — the content-verification that was meant to detect collision/corruption is bypassed because neither writer's ReadEntireFileIfExists sees the other's file. (2) An attacker who can write to the store directory can win a race window to place arbitrary content at a hash address, then have the legitimate writer's rename fail to detect the substitution.
attack_path: 1. Process A calls PutPayload for body_hash H, ReadEntireFileIfExists returns empty. 2. Attacker writes a crafted payload file at the hash H path between the read and the rename. 3. Process A's DurablyWriteFile renames its temp file over the attacker's file, or the attacker's write replaces Process A's file — depending on timing, either attacker or legitimate content wins. 4. Subsequent GetPayload will re-hash and detect the mismatch — but DurablyCreateNewFile (which uses link() for publish-once semantics) is NOT used by the main put paths, only by specific sidecar flows.
evidence: runtime/platform/checkpoint/durable_writer.cc:204-261 — DurablyCreateNewFile exists with link()-based atomicity but is not used by PutPayload/PutManifest
remediation: Use DurablyCreateNewFile (with link() semantics) for all content-addressed Put operations instead of DurablyWriteFile. When DurablyCreateNewFile returns AlreadyExists, read the existing file and verify content matches. This eliminates the TOCTOU window because link() is atomic — if two writers race, exactly one succeeds and the other gets EEXIST. The existing DurablyCreateNewFile already implements this pattern correctly.
poc_video_notes: Run two concurrent PutPayload calls for the same hash address with different payloads. Instrument the code with a sleep between ReadEntireFileIfExists and DurablyWriteFile to widen the race window. Show that both succeed without error and the final content is non-deterministic.

title: Decision engine appends event before projection, creating a log-desync window on projection failure
description: StatelessDecisionEngine::Decide() appends the user's request event to the log at line 62-66 *before* running projection and inference. If projector->Project() or decider_runner_->Generate() subsequently fails, the user event has already been durably appended to the event log, but no corresponding model response event exists. The next Decide() call will see this orphaned event, potentially projecting it twice (once as part of the checkpoint's event range from the failed call, and again in the new call's range). There is no rollback mechanism for the append-only log. Furthermore, the appended event uses `clock_->NowMicros()` as a fallback timestamp when `timestamp_us` is not provided and `allow_wall_clock_timestamps` is true — in a replay scenario, this creates non-deterministic timestamps that break the deterministic projection guarantee.
impact: Partial failure during Decide() leaves the event log in an inconsistent state: user events without matching model responses. This can cause (1) downstream replay auditors to see different event ranges than expected, (2) the correction protocol to emit spurious drift corrections, and (3) in the wall-clock timestamp fallback path, non-reproducible timestamps that make exact-replay auditing fundamentally impossible for those events.
attack_path: 1. Attacker submits a request that passes validation but causes the inference runner to fail (e.g. oversized input that exceeds model context, or network timeout to an external model). 2. The user event is durably appended. 3. The function returns an error — caller retries with the same request. 4. The event log now has duplicate user events. 5. Replay auditor computes a different projection (because it sees duplicated events) and emits a correction. 6. Repeated exploitation fills the event log with orphaned events, degrading projection quality and triggering correction storms.
evidence: runtime/dpm/stateless_decision_engine.cc:72-85 — projection and inference that can fail after append
remediation: Restructure Decide() to run projection and inference first, then append both events atomically (or in sequence). If two-phase append is not feasible with the append-only log model, implement a compensating mechanism: mark the user event as 'tentative' and only finalize it when the model response is also ready. Alternatively, append both events together as a transaction. Remove or gate the wall-clock timestamp fallback more strictly.
poc_video_notes: Call Decide() with a config that causes the inference runner to return an error. Show the event log has the user event but no model event. Call Decide() again with the same request. Show the log now has duplicate user events. Run a replay auditor and show it detects drift.

title: Liboqs shared library loaded via dlopen with attacker-influenceable path, enabling code execution
description: The LibOqsApi::Load() function opens the liboqs shared library using dlopen() with a path that defaults to `liboqs.so` (a relative name) when library_path is empty (line 92). When a relative library name is passed to dlopen(), the dynamic linker searches LD_LIBRARY_PATH, RUNPATH, and the standard system paths. An attacker who can control LD_LIBRARY_PATH or place a malicious `liboqs.so` in a directory that appears earlier in the search path can have arbitrary code executed with the DPM runtime's privileges. The LibOqsAuditCertificateSigner constructor and GenerateLibOqsMlDsaKeyPair both accept an empty library_path and default to this unsafe behavior.
impact: An attacker who can influence the library search path (via environment variable manipulation, symlink placement in the working directory, or shared filesystem) can substitute a malicious shared library that will be loaded by the DPM runtime. The malicious library's code runs in the DPM process context with full access to signing keys, event data, and checkpoint stores. This enables forging of audit certificate signatures, exfiltration of private keys, and arbitrary code execution.
attack_path: 1. Attacker places a malicious `liboqs.so` in the DPM runtime's working directory or a path in LD_LIBRARY_PATH. 2. DPM runtime creates a LibOqsAuditCertificateSigner with default (empty) library_path. 3. Sign() or Verify() calls LibOqsApi::Load(), which calls dlopen('liboqs.so', RTLD_NOW|RTLD_LOCAL). 4. Dynamic linker finds the attacker's library first. 5. Attacker's code executes in the DPM process, with access to secret_key material passed to Sign().
evidence: runtime/platform/audit/liboqs_audit_certificate_signer.cc:100 — dlopen(path.c_str(), RTLD_NOW | RTLD_LOCAL) with potentially relative path
runtime/platform/audit/liboqs_audit_certificate_signer.cc:281 — Sign() loads library on every call, re-executing dlopen
remediation: Require library_path to be an absolute path. In DefaultLibOqsPath(), return a fully-qualified path (e.g. '/usr/lib/liboqs.so' or a build-time configured path). Add validation in DynamicLibrary::Open() that rejects relative paths. Consider loading the library once at process startup and caching the handle rather than reloading on every Sign()/Verify() call.
poc_video_notes: Set LD_LIBRARY_PATH to a directory containing a malicious liboqs.so that logs all calls. Create a LibOqsAuditCertificateSigner with default path. Call Sign() and show the malicious library's code executing.

title: Case-insensitive ASCII-only fact matching allows correction bypass via Unicode homoglyphs
description: The correction fact-matching in MatchRevocationForEvent() uses a simple ASCII-only LowerAscii() function (lines 52-60) that only lowercases A-Z. The invalidated fact search uses `lowered_payload.find(fact.lowered)` for substring matching. This means: (1) Unicode homoglyphs (e.g. Cyrillic 'а' U+0430 vs Latin 'a' U+0061) are not normalized, allowing an event payload to contain visually identical text that does not match the correction's invalidated_facts. (2) The substring matching is a simple find() without word boundaries, so both over-matching (matching inside longer words) and under-matching (missing homoglyphs) are possible. An attacker who controls event content can use Unicode substitution to embed facts that visually appear to match correction directives but are not revoked.
impact: Correction directives that should revoke events containing specific forbidden facts can be bypassed by using Unicode homoglyphs or mixed-script text in event payloads. This means an attacker can craft events that visually contain invalidated facts but survive the correction filter, causing stale or forbidden information to flow into the projector's active evidence view and ultimately into DPM decisions.
attack_path: 1. Audit system emits a correction with invalidated_facts=['classified data leak']. 2. Attacker submits a new event with payload containing 'сlassified data leak' (Cyrillic 'с' instead of Latin 'c'). 3. LowerAscii does not normalize the Cyrillic character. 4. find() does not match the invalidated fact. 5. The event is NOT revoked and appears in the active evidence view. 6. The projector sees the un-revoked event and includes the forbidden fact in the projected memory.
evidence: runtime/dpm/active_evidence_view.cc:106 — case folding applied to payload
remediation: Replace the ASCII-only LowerAscii() with a Unicode-aware normalization function (e.g. ICU case folding + NFKC normalization). Apply confusable-detection (Unicode TR39 skeleton algorithm) to both the payload and the invalidated facts before matching. Consider using exact content hashes of event payloads in the correction protocol rather than substring matching.
poc_video_notes: Create a correction with invalidated_facts=['secret']. Submit an event with payload containing 'ѕесrеt' (using Cyrillic lookalikes). Show that the event is not revoked in the ActiveEvidenceView output.

title: Dependent manifest index is not integrity-protected, enabling checkpoint chain manipulation
description: MaybePersistDependentManifestIndex() (lines 98-132) maintains a sidecar index file mapping parent manifest hashes to their dependent (child) manifest hashes. This index is a plain-text file of hex hashes separated by newlines, with no integrity protection (no MAC, no signature, no content hash). The index is written via DurablyWriteFile (overwrite semantics, not DurablyCreateNewFile), and is read by ListDependentManifests() and transitively by InvalidatedCheckpointClosure() in the replay auditor. An attacker who can modify this index file can add or remove entries, causing the invalidation closure to miss dependent checkpoints or include unrelated ones.
impact: Manipulation of the dependent manifest index allows an attacker to: (1) Remove entries so that when a correction invalidates a checkpoint, its descendants are not included in the invalidation closure — effectively keeping stale checkpoints alive. (2) Add spurious entries to cause legitimate checkpoints to be incorrectly invalidated, creating a denial of service for the correction flow. The InvalidatedCheckpointClosure function in projection_replay_auditor.cc directly trusts this index.
attack_path: 1. Attacker modifies a .idx file in the deps/ directory, removing the hash of a descendant checkpoint that depends on a known-bad parent. 2. Replay auditor detects drift on the parent checkpoint and calls InvalidatedCheckpointClosure(). 3. ListDependentManifests returns the modified index, missing the descendant. 4. The descendant checkpoint is not included in the invalidation set. 5. A subsequent decision request loads the un-invalidated descendant checkpoint, using stale projected memory.
remediation: Add integrity protection to the dependent manifest index: either (1) compute an HMAC or hash over the index content and store it alongside, verifying on read; or (2) use the fallback InvalidatedCheckpointClosureByManifestScan (which verifies against actual manifest content) as the primary path rather than trusting the index. At minimum, use DurablyCreateNewFile for append-only index semantics.
poc_video_notes: Create a chain of checkpoints A -> B. Modify A's .idx file to remove B's hash. Trigger a correction that invalidates A. Show that B is not in the invalidation closure.

title: Secret key material persists in memory without secure erasure
description: The LibOqsSignatureKeyPair struct stores the secret_key as a std::string (liboqs_audit_certificate_signer.h line 32). When the signer object is destroyed or the string is reassigned, the secret key bytes remain in the process's heap memory until the allocator reuses that page. std::string's destructor does not zero-fill the buffer. This is compounded by the fact that Sign() loads the library and creates a new OQS_SIG on every call (line 281-283), but the secret_key string member persists for the lifetime of the signer object. If the process memory is dumped (core dump, /proc/pid/mem, side-channel), the post-quantum signing key is recoverable.
impact: Post-quantum secret key material remains in process memory after use without secure erasure. In environments where process memory may be inspectable (shared hosting, container escapes, core dumps enabled), this allows recovery of ML-DSA signing keys that could be used to forge audit certificate signatures.
attack_path: 1. DPM runtime creates a LibOqsAuditCertificateSigner with a valid ML-DSA key pair. 2. Signer is used and eventually destroyed (or the process crashes). 3. Attacker accesses the core dump or process memory image. 4. Attacker searches for ML-DSA key material (known size: 2560 bytes for ML-DSA-44, 4032 for ML-DSA-65, 4896 for ML-DSA-87). 5. Attacker uses recovered key to forge audit certificates.
evidence: runtime/platform/audit/liboqs_audit_certificate_signer.cc:289-295 — secret key passed to liboqs sign function via data pointer
remediation: Use a secure-erase wrapper around the secret_key storage (e.g. a custom allocator that calls memset_s/explicit_bzero on deallocation). Add a destructor to LibOqsSignatureKeyPair that explicitly zeros the secret_key buffer before it is freed. Consider using a memory-locked (mlock) allocation for the key material to prevent it from being swapped to disk.
poc_video_notes: Create and destroy a LibOqsAuditCertificateSigner. Take a heap dump of the process. Search for the known public key bytes to locate the memory region. Show the secret key bytes are still present in the adjacent memory.

title: Hash256::FromHex returns zero-hash without error indication when ok pointer is null
description: Hash256::FromHex() (hasher.cc lines 49-66) takes an optional `bool* ok` parameter. When the input hex string is malformed (wrong length or invalid characters), the function returns a zero-initialized Hash256 and sets `*ok = false` — but only if `ok` is non-null. If a caller passes `ok = nullptr` (which is valid since it's a pointer parameter), the function silently returns a zero hash with no error indication. A zero Hash256 is a valid value that could collide with the IsZeroHash() sentinel used in the replay auditor and elsewhere, creating confusion between 'parse error' and 'actual zero hash'.
impact: Callers that invoke FromHex() without providing an `ok` output parameter will silently receive a zero hash on parse failure. If this zero hash is then used as a lookup key in the checkpoint store or DAG store, it could either (1) cause a NotFound error (benign) or (2) match an existing entry at the zero address (if one exists from initialization or a bug). The replay auditor uses IsZeroHash() as a sentinel to detect missing configuration — a silently-zeroed hash from a parse error would be incorrectly flagged as 'missing config' rather than 'corrupted hash input'.
evidence: runtime/platform/hash/hasher.cc:49-66 — FromHex returns zero hash silently when ok is null
runtime/platform/hash/hasher.cc:53 — `if (ok) *ok = false;` — no error path when ok is null
remediation: Change FromHex() to return absl::StatusOr<Hash256> instead of using an output parameter. This makes error handling mandatory and eliminates the silent-failure path. If the API cannot be changed, require ok to be non-null (add an assertion or return a distinct sentinel value for parse failure).
poc_video_notes: Call Hash256::FromHex with invalid hex and ok=nullptr. Show the returned hash is zero. Pass this hash to IsZeroHash() and show it returns true, masking the parse error as a missing-config condition.
